Vocabulary
The Dubai Shopping Festival
bargain
something bought for less than its usual price
boutique
a small fashionable shop that sells special or expensive goods
brand
a name given by the maker to a product or range of products
counterfeit
made to look like the original but not genuine; fake
designer
made by a famous fashion designer; expensive and fashionable
genuine
real, authentic, not fake or counterfeit
luxury
great comfort and expense; something pleasant but not essential
material
the substance used to make something, such as cotton, leather, or silk
pattern
a repeated decorative design on fabric or paper
retail
the sale of goods to the public in shops, not for resale
signature
a distinctive feature that identifies a particular brand or designer
trend
a general direction of change in fashion or opinion
vintage
old but high quality; from a previous era
wardrobe
a person's entire collection of clothes

Grammar
Adjective Clauses with Subject Relative Pronouns
who / that — for people
Use when the relative pronoun is the subject of the adjective clause and refers to a person.
The woman who/that designed this dress is from Italy.
My friend who/that lives in Dubai loves shopping festivals.
which / that — for things
Use when the relative pronoun is the subject of the adjective clause and refers to a thing.
The bag which/that costs $2,000 is made by hand.
This store sells shoes that/which are made from recycled plastic.
whose — for possession
Use to show that something belongs to a person or thing. It replaces a possessive adjective (his, her, its, their).
The designer whose signature is on this label is very famous.
I met a customer whose wardrobe was entirely vintage.
Important: The relative pronoun replaces the subject of the adjective clause. Do not repeat the subject!

❌ The man who he designed the building is my uncle.
✅ The man who designed the building is my uncle.
Pronunciation: Intonation Patterns in Relative Clauses

In defining clauses (no commas, essential information), the voice flows smoothly into the clause without a pause.

In non-defining clauses (with commas, extra information), we usually pause slightly and use a falling intonation at the end of the clause.

Example: "My favorite boutique, which is in the old city center, sells vintage clothing." (pause before "which," fall at "center")

→ The designer won an award.
I bought a scarf. It has a beautiful floral pattern.
→ I bought a scarf .
The customer complained about the price. His wallet was stolen.
→ The customer complained about the price.
The store sells genuine products. It is located in the mall.
→ The store sells genuine products.
The sales assistant helped me. She speaks three languages.
→ The sales assistant helped me.

Reading
Every Shoe Tells a Story

👠 Every Shoe Tells a Story

Look down at your feet. The shoes you are wearing right now say more about you than you might think. A team of psychologists at the University of Kansas recently published a study showing that strangers can guess a person's personality, income, and even political views simply by looking at their shoes. The researchers photographed the footwear of 200 volunteers and asked another group to describe the wearers. The results were surprisingly accurate.

People who wear practical, comfortable shoes tend to describe themselves as agreeable and calm. Those who prefer ankle boots are often more aggressive and competitive. Volunteers who chose colorful, well-maintained footwear were generally identified as more extroverted and fashion-conscious. Meanwhile, participants who wore cheap, worn-out shoes were frequently judged as anxious or insecure—though the study notes this can be unfair, as financial hardship may be the real reason.

Shoes also carry cultural meaning. In Japan, the tradition of removing shoes at the door reflects values of cleanliness and respect. In many parts of India, leather shoes that cover the toes are worn for formal occasions, while simpler sandals are for everyday life. The Maasai people of East Africa make sandals from old car tires, a design that is both practical and symbolic of modern adaptation.

Your profession leaves its mark as well. A chef wears thick, non-slip shoes that survive long hours on wet floors. A nurse chooses sneakers that cushion her feet through twelve-hour shifts. A construction worker depends on heavy boots with steel toes. Each pair is a tool, chosen for function before fashion.

But the story is not always simple. Some people who can afford luxury brands choose to wear simple, unbranded shoes. Some collectors own hundreds of pairs, while minimalists prefer just one. The psychologists who conducted the study warn us not to judge too quickly. "One pair of shoes is only a single chapter," they write. "To read the whole story, you have to look at the person wearing them."

Writing
Present and Defend an Argument
Writing Strategy — Making a Successful Argument:
1. Thesis: State your opinion clearly in one sentence.
2. Reasons: Give 2-3 reasons with evidence or examples.
3. Counterargument: Address the other side, then explain why your view is stronger.
4. Conclusion: Restate your opinion and give a final, powerful thought.

Model Argument: Quality Over Quantity

Buying fewer, better-quality clothes is better than following fast fashion trends. First, the fashion industry is one of the world's largest polluters, and cheap clothes are often thrown away after only a few washes. A genuine wool coat that lasts ten years is better for the environment than ten synthetic coats that fall apart in one season. Second, a smaller wardrobe of classic pieces actually saves money over time. A well-made leather bag may cost more at first, but it will not need to be replaced. Some people argue that fast fashion is affordable and allows everyone to follow trends. However, the low price hides the true cost of environmental damage and poor working conditions in factories. Therefore, consumers should choose quality over quantity and build a wardrobe that lasts.

Exercise B — Choose a topic and write your argument
Outline: Thesis → Reason 1 + Evidence → Reason 2 + Evidence → Counterargument + Response → Conclusion

Speaking
Fashion Survey & Reacting to Opinions
Exercise A — Fashion Survey

Walk around the class. Ask your classmates these questions. Note their answers.

1. Do you care about brands when you buy clothes?
2. Would you pay more for a genuine product?
3. Have you ever bought a counterfeit item?
4. Is comfort more important than fashion?
5. Would you wear vintage clothes?
Speaking Strategy — Reacting to Someone Else's Point of View:

Agreeing: "I completely agree." / "That's a good point." / "I feel the same way."
Partial agreement: "I see your point, but..." / "That's true to some extent. However..." / "I agree up to a point, but..."
Politely disagreeing: "I'm not sure I agree with that." / "You might be right, but what about...?" / "I take your point, but have you considered...?" / "I understand what you're saying, but from my perspective..."
Roleplay: Fashion vs. Comfort

Student A (Fashion-Forward): You believe that appearance is important. You think people should follow trends and buy quality designer pieces. Use the survey results to support your view.

Student B (Comfort-First): You believe that comfort and practicality are more important than fashion. You think spending money on expensive brands is wasteful. React to Student A's opinions.

Expanding Your Fluency
The Style Challenge
Scenario: The Return

Work in pairs. Student A bought a bag at a market. At home, they realized it is counterfeit. Student B is the shop owner who says "All sales are final." Use adjective clauses and argument phrases to reach an agreement.

Student A: The Customer

You want to return the bag. Describe the bag that you bought. Explain why you believe the seller whose stall is near the entrance sold you a fake. You want a refund.

Student B: The Shop Owner

You never said the bag was genuine. The price was very low, which should have told the customer it was not a designer item. However, you want good reviews. Offer store credit instead of cash.

Your agreement: The customer will receive . The shop owner will in the future.
